snapshot.title: UPSC Economy: Industry & Infrastructure
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Economy Hook: IP 1991: LPG. 8 Core industries. MSME: Investment+Turnover. IIP: 2011-12. Maharatna: Max Autonomy. Gati Shakti: Logistics.

quick_notes.title: Industrial Policy 1991
quick_notes.detail: LPG Reforms (Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization). Ended "License Raj". Reduced public sector reserved areas.
quick_notes.explanation: Industrial Policy 1991 was a set of government rules announced in 1991 to change how industries worked in India. It is also called the LPG Reforms, where LPG stands for Liberalization (removing government controls), Privatization (allowing private companies to own and run businesses), and Globalization (opening the Indian economy to foreign trade and investment). This policy ended the "License Raj", which was a system where businesses needed many government permissions (licenses) to start or expand. It also reduced the list of industries that were reserved only for the public sector (government-owned companies), meaning private companies could now enter those areas.

quick_notes.title: Index of Industrial Production (IIP)
quick_notes.detail: Measures short-term changes in volume of production. 8 Core Industries account for ~40% weightage (Refinery products, Electricity, Steel, Coal, Crude oil, Natural gas, Cement, Fertilizers).
quick_notes.explanation: Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is a number that measures the short-term changes in the volume of goods produced by factories, mines, and power plants in India. It is calculated and released every month by the Central Statistics Office (CSO), which is a government department that collects and publishes economic data. The IIP is like a speedometer for the industrial sector, showing if the industry is growing or shrinking. Eight Core Industries, which are the most important industrial sectors like Refinery products, Electricity, Steel, Coal, Crude oil, Natural gas, Cement, and Fertilizers, together make up about 40% of the total weight of the IIP, meaning they have a big impact on the final number. For example, if a lot more electricity is generated in a month, the IIP will increase because electricity has a large weight in the calculation. This index helps banks, businesses, and the government understand how the economy is doing in the short term.

quick_notes.title: CPSE Categorization
quick_notes.detail: Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna. Based on profit, net worth, and global presence. (e.g., ONGC, NTPC are Maharatnas).
quick_notes.explanation: A Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE) is a company owned by the government of India. The government gives certain CPSEs special statuses called Maharatna, Navratna, and Miniratna based on how much profit they make, how high their net worth (total assets minus liabilities) is, and whether they have a strong global presence (operations in other countries). For example, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) are given the Maharatna status, which is the highest category. These categories help the companies get more freedom to make big investment decisions without needing the government's approval for every step.

quick_notes.title: MSME Definition (New)
quick_notes.detail: Based on Investment and Turnover. Micro (<1cr/5cr), Small (<10cr/50cr), Medium (<50cr/250cr).
quick_notes.explanation: MSME stands for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises. The new definition classifies these businesses based on two things: their total investment in plant and machinery or equipment, and their annual turnover, which is the total money they make in a year from sales. A Micro enterprise is one with an investment of less than 1 crore rupees and a turnover of less than 5 crore rupees. A Small enterprise has an investment of less than 10 crore rupees and a turnover of less than 50 crore rupees. A Medium enterprise has an investment of less than 50 crore rupees and a turnover of less than 250 crore rupees. This classification helps the government decide which businesses qualify for special loans, subsidies, and other support programs.

quick_notes.title: Infrastructure Initiatives
quick_notes.detail: PM Gati Shakti (Multimodal connectivity). Bharatmala (Roads). Sagarmala (Ports). PLI (Production Linked Incentive) to boost manufacturing.
quick_notes.explanation: PM Gati Shakti, which stands for Prime Minister Gati Shakti, is a government program that creates a digital map to plan and connect different types of transport, like roads, railways, and ports, so that goods and people can move faster. Bharatmala is a project to build and improve highways and roads across India, especially in border areas and to connect smaller towns. Sagarmala is a scheme focused on developing India's ports and the areas around them to make shipping and trade more efficient. PLI, or Production Linked Incentive, is a policy where the government gives money to companies that make more products in India, encouraging them to boost manufacturing. Together, these initiatives aim to improve the country's infrastructure, reduce travel time for goods, and create more jobs by making it easier to produce and transport things.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Physical Engine'. Industrial growth and robust infrastructure are the keys to a 'Viksit Bharat'. We explore the Industrial Policy Resolutions, the 'Maharatna/Navratna' status, and the modern push for Gati Shakti and PLI schemes. For UPSC, focus on the 'Core Industries', 'MSME definitions', and the 'Logistic Performance Index'. This is the real-world application of economic theory.
